title: Plan Your Exit Before Day One
hook_text: PLAN YOUR EXIT BEFORE YOU START

beats.say: The best time to plan leaving a business is before it even exists.
beats.visual: A silhouette of a person standing at the edge of a high-rise concrete roof at blue hour, looking out over a foggy skyline.

beats.say: Most founders accidentally build a job, then get trapped working 70 hours a week.
beats.visual: Low-angle shot of a lone suit jacket hung over a chair in a dark, empty glass skyscraper at night, cold fluorescent lighting.

beats.say: You might assume buyers pay top dollar for your personal hustle and hard work.
beats.visual: Extreme close-up of hands typing rapidly on a dark keyboard under a single sodium desk lamp, deep shadow surrounding.

beats.say: That's wrong. Nobody buys a business that breaks the minute you step out the door.
beats.visual: Extreme wide shot of an empty warehouse floor with wet asphalt reflecting harsh overhead spotlights.

beats.say: So how do you build a company that someone will actually pay you cash to own?
beats.visual: High-angle perspective looking down an endless dark stairwell, illuminated only by blue emergency lights.

beats.say: Step one is deciding your exit strategy before you spend your first dollar.
beats.visual: Macro shot of a leather fountain pen resting beside blank blueprint paper on a heavy wooden desk in low light.

beats.say: Investor Dan Peña lists exit planning as a core rule. By his account, he built a $450 million company.
beats.visual: Silhouette of a figure walking down a long, rain-slick stone corridor in an ancient castle courtyard at twilight.

beats.say: He says true wealth comes from making yourself replaceable, not staying indispensable.
beats.visual: Low-angle camera looking up at massive steel financial district towers framed against a stormy, dark sky.

beats.say: Step two is documenting every single task so anyone can run the operations without you.
beats.visual: Close-up shot from behind showing gloved hands flipping through a thick black binder under cold fluorescent light.

beats.say: Here's the honest catch: using borrowed money to scale fast means you owe debt during bad months.
beats.visual: Extreme wide shot of a solitary car driving down a deserted dark highway under heavy fog at night.

beats.say: When systems generate cash without your labor, you don't just own a job, you own a sellable asset.
beats.visual: Low angle of a sleek black luxury sedan parked on rain-wet pavement under the glow of a single streetlamp.

beats.say: Decide how you'll leave before day one. Follow for the money rules school never taught you.
beats.visual: Extreme wide silhouette of a person walking across a dark concrete bridge, mist cutting across the distance.

caption:
Buyers pay for systems, not your personal hustle. Here is why you plan the exit before day one.

#money #business #wealth #financialfreedom #exitstrategy
description: Most business owners build a job they can never leave. By planning your exit on day one and building systems that run without you, you create a sellable asset instead of a trap.
first_comment: If you started a business today, would you aim to sell it or keep it forever?

facts.claim: Dan Peña claims his oil company reached a $450 million market value.
facts.basis: Research brief: Great Western Resources reached a $450 million market value by his account.

facts.claim: Plan the exit is Peña's 7th step.
facts.basis: Research brief: His 7 Steps to Super Success includes 'plan the exit' from day one.

facts.claim: Borrowing money creates fixed debt obligations regardless of business performance.
facts.basis: Research brief honest catch: Buying or scaling a business with borrowed money means debt is owed even during bad years.

loop_map.stakes: Founders build businesses that trap them for 70 hours a week.
loop_map.big_question: How do you build a business someone will actually pay cash to buy?
loop_map.assume: Buyers pay for founder hustle and past revenue.
loop_map.reveal: Buyers pay for automated systems that operate without the founder.
